(There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.text:
The review of PR #2549 found 9 issues. The first two can make the trail report "clean" when it shouldn't be, so I'd fix those before merging.

**Correctness (fix before merge)**
1. **Streamed text runs together** (`review/dump.go:193`). `joinAssistantText` only puts a newline between two text events if one of them isn't a delta. So separate Pi messages, or a retry attempt's partial output, get glued together with no break. A verdict like `request changes` then no longer starts a line, `proseReportsFindings` misses it, and an empty comments array gets treated as clean.
2. **Labeled verdicts are no longer recognized** (`review/trail_report.go:167`). `proseReportsFindings` only checks for bare prefixes. Text like `**Verdict:** request changes`, `Nits:`, `Issues:` or `[p1]` followed by `"comments":[]` is now treated as clean. This undoes the fix in e2df2bb5d (`startsWithFeedbackLabel`).
3. **One blank comment discards all of them** (`trail_report.go:148`). If any comment has an empty body, `decodeTrailComments` rejects the whole array. The code then falls back to prose that has already had the JSON removed, so valid findings are lost. If the judge also wrote no prose, the raw JSON gets posted as the finding instead. The old code just skipped blank comments.
4. **The judge's empty result gets overridden** (`trail_report.go:92`). When the judge returns zero comments, every high-severity reviewer comment is posted anyway, with no dedup. So a false positive the judge dropped still gets posted, and two reviewers flagging the same thing posts it twice. If the judge returns a single low comment instead, all the highs are dropped, so the two cases behave inconsistently.
5. **JSON is stripped when it isn't the contract** (`cmd.go:1644`). `combinedReviewNarratives` removes a trailing JSON object even when it isn't valid contract JSON (ok=false). `stripTrailJSON` doesn't do that, so a reviewer's evidence snippet (say, a `package.json` object) disappears from the trail post but still shows in the local dump.

**Efficiency and design**
6. **Findings reach the judge twice** (`synthesis_prompt.go:67`). The judge prompt includes each reviewer's full narrative, JSON contract line included, so every finding appears both as a bullet and as JSON. Applying `stripTrailJSON` here, as `dump.go` already does, fixes it.
7. **Pi-specific fix in shared code** (`agent/pi/reviewer.go:90`). The shared `Delta` flag works around a Pi-only problem. The Pi parser could instead collect deltas per message and emit one block at `message_end`. That keeps message boundaries, which also fixes #1. The TUI (`tui_detail.go`, `tui_model.go`) still renders each delta as its own block.
8. **Duplicated rules** (`trail_report.go:183`). `isListItem` and `isHighTrailSeverity` repeat what `topLevelBulletText` and `normalizeReviewTrailSeverity` in `review_bridge.go` already do, and they've already drifted: the new ones don't handle `nit`/`p3` or strip punctuation.
9. **Internal wording in user output** (`cmd.go:1609`). Users see `Nothing to report (reviewer JSON: 0 comments from 1 reviewer(s))`. A plain "no findings" line would do.

I haven't checked these by hand or run tests. They're the reviewer's analysis of the source. I also didn't check the diff against your Review Lessons files.

**Proposed lesson** for `Review Lessons/cli.md` (I'll add it only if you approve):
- "When rewriting a parser or classifier, keep the earlier fixes' regression cases (for example, feedback labels like `Nits:`) as tests for the new implementation; a rewrite can silently drop handling that only those cases cover."

Do you want me to fix #1 through #6 on this branch? If so, I'll write a short plan first.

content.text:
I checked all 9 findings against the code at the PR head (5741eb83b). Seven hold up: four are real bugs (#1, #2, #3, #6) and three are smaller design or cleanup points (#7, #8, #9). The other two (#4, #5) describe behavior the code comments say was chosen deliberately, so they're your call rather than bugs. I tested #1, #2, #3 and #5 by running copies of the functions in the scratchpad against the reported inputs, so no repo files changed. The rest I checked by reading the source.

| # | Finding | Verdict | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Streamed text from separate messages runs together | **Confirmed, and new in this PR** | Two message streams separated by a tool call joined as `"I'll read the diff.request changes — …"`. The prose check then returned false, so the empty comments array was accepted as clean. On `main` each delta got its own line, so the clean check never had this problem. |
| 2 | Labeled verdicts are treated as clean | **Confirmed** | `proseReportsFindings` returned false for `**Verdict:** request changes — …`, `Nits: rename x`, `Issues: …` and `[p1] …`. `findings.go` (added in e2df2bb5d) was deleted by 5741eb83b, so the label handling is gone. Lower impact now: it only matters when a model writes findings in prose but returns an empty comments array, which is exactly the case this check exists for. |
| 3 | One blank comment loses all of them | **Confirmed** | Prose `approve` plus JSON with one real high comment and one blank-body comment gave `ok=false`, 0 comments, prose `"approve"`. The fallback then posts a generic "approve" verdict and the real finding is gone. `main` skipped blank entries instead. |
| 4 | Judge's empty result is overridden by reviewer highs | **Deliberate, but has a real gap** | The comment at `trail_report.go:84` says this is on purpose: an empty judge result can't erase a reviewer's high-severity finding. Two parts are still real: there's no dedup, so two reviewers flagging the same thing post it twice; and if the judge returns even one low comment, every reviewer high is dropped. That inconsistency is the part worth deciding on. |
| 5 | JSON is stripped when it isn't the contract | **Deliberate, low impact** | Reproduced: `splitTrailJSON` removes non-contract JSON from the posted prose, while `stripTrailJSON` keeps it for the local dump. The doc comment says this is on purpose, so malformed contract JSON is never posted as finding text. Losing a quoted config snippet is the cost of that choice. |
| 6 | Reviewer JSON sent to the judge twice | **Confirmed, and new in this PR** | `synthesis_prompt.go:67` uses `joinAssistantText` without `stripTrailJSON`. This PR is what adds the JSON line to reviewer output (`prompt.go`), so the judge now sees each finding twice, plus an example of the output format inside data it's told to treat as untrusted. One-line fix. `manifest.go:684` also stores the JSON line in the narrative; the reviewer didn't flag that, and it matters less. |
| 7 | Pi-only fix put in shared code | **Valid design point** | Accumulating text per message in the Pi parser and emitting it once at `message_end` would fix #1 without the shared `Delta` flag. The reviewer's claim about the TUI is wrong, though: the TUI already showed one block per delta on `main`, so that isn't a regression. |
| 8 | Duplicated bullet and severity rules | **Valid, minor** | The drift is real: `isHighTrailSeverity` strips only `[]`, while `normalizeReviewTrailSeverity` strips `[](){}:*_`. Fixing it isn't simple reuse, though: `review` can't import `cli`, so the normalizer would have to move into `review`. |
| 9 | Internal wording in user output | **Confirmed, cosmetic** | `cmd.go:1609` prints `Nothing to report (reviewer JSON: 0 comments from N reviewer(s))`. |

**My recommendation:**
- **Fix:** #1 (ideally the #7 way, in the Pi parser), #3 (skip blank entries like `main` did), #6 (one line), and #2 (restore the label and verdict-prefix checks, with the e2df2bb5d cases as tests).
- **Decide:** #4. The simplest consistent rule is "dedup reviewer highs, and add them whenever the judge didn't already report them," or else drop the override and trust the judge.
- **Leave or tidy:** #5, #8, #9.

Which of these do you want fixed?

Trail: https://entire.io/gh/MuskanPaliwal/cli/trails/12

When a reviewer approves a change with nothing to report, `entire review` posts that approval to the Trail as a finding. The Trail then shows an "Unspecified finding" for a review that found nothing.

`reviewTrailFindingInputs` looks for structured comments or Markdown finding bullets in the reviewer output. A clean approval such as

```text
approve - no actionable findings
```

has neither, so the fallback posts the whole output as one severity-less, whole-change comment.

This originally surfaced alongside a Claude stream parsing bug that made Codex the only successful reviewer. #2699 has since fixed the parser. The clean-verdict behavior is independent of it and still reproduces with any reviewer that returns a plain approval.

## What changed

`maybePostReviewToTrail` now skips posting when the review is clean and prints the existing "Nothing to report" notice instead. The check runs before the reviewer outputs are joined:

- With a synthesized verdict, that verdict must be clean.
- Without one (single reviewer, or synthesis produced nothing), every reviewer's output must be clean on its own. One approving reviewer cannot hide another reviewer's findings.

Output is clean when its last non-empty line is an unqualified `approve` and no line is a non-clean verdict. Prompts put the verdict first, so a trailing "Approve once that is fixed." cannot override an earlier `request changes`.

Accepted as clean:

- plain approvals: `approve`, `APPROVE.`, `Approved.`
- Markdown emphasis or headings: `**approve** - ...`, `## approve`
- an approve whose reason says nothing needs fixing: `approve - no actionable defects found.`, `approve with nothing to report`, `approve! looks good.`
- reasoning or chatter before the final verdict line, as long as it cites no file:line

Still posted:

- `request changes`, anywhere in the output
- approvals carrying feedback or a condition: `approve with nits`, `approve with notes`, `approve (nits: ...)`, `approve, but ...`, `approve once ...`, `approved pending ...`, `looks good, though ...`
- any other approve reason, since it may be feedback: `approve - rename x for clarity`, `approve - no tests cover the retry path`
- any finding-shaped line, at any indentation: a bullet, a numbered item, or a severity marker such as `[high]`
- any line containing a file:line pointer such as `retry.go:42`, including the approve reason itself
- labelled or bulleted verdicts the parser does not recognize: `Verdict: approve`, `- approve`
- prose after the verdict line
- a reviewer whose output has no verdict line

When unsure, it posts. A false "clean" would hide a real finding, while a false "not clean" only restores the previous behavior.

`reviewTrailFindingInputs` is unchanged. Its existing test now uses a `request changes` input, since a clean approval no longer reaches it.

## Tests

In `review/posttrail_test.go`, using real single- and multi-reviewer run summaries:

- `TestMaybePostReviewToTrailSkipsCleanVerdicts`: clean synthesized verdicts, a reviewer with preamble before the verdict, and two clean reviewers (one with its own `## Summary` heading) are not posted.
- `TestMaybePostReviewToTrailPostsNonCleanVerdicts`: the non-clean forms above, including approve reasons that carry feedback, plus one reviewer requesting changes or giving no verdict while another approves, are posted.

## Scope

This does not change review prompts, reviewer failure policy, synthesis, Trail API types, or server rendering.

 - Reviewers run the profile task.
 - Multi-reviewer profiles run reviewers concurrently, then run one judge.
 - Results are printed and saved locally; `output: "trail"` also posts findings to the branch trail.
+- In trail mode, reviewers and the judge end their output with a JSON line, `{"summary":...,"comments":[...]}` (`trail_report.go`). The instruction is appended last, after profile and per-run text, and is skipped for a verbatim `prompt` override. Posting reads that line instead of interpreting prose:
+  - `"comments":[]` posts nothing, unless the prose has a list item, a severity tag, or a `request changes` / `approve with nits` verdict. A judge `[]` also does not hide a reviewer's own high-severity comment.

 - A bare non-interactive `entire review` does not auto-run a profile. Automation should pass a profile name.
 - Profile selection is positional/`--profile` → `review_default_profile` → `general` → the only configured profile.

lastPrompt: but it does have some out of scope things right?

content.text:
Yes. The biggest issue is that the PR has grown well past what its title and description promise. The description still says:

> This does not change review prompts, reviewer failure policy, synthesis, Trail API types, or server rendering.
> `reviewTrailFindingInputs` is unchanged.

Both statements were true of the early commits. The last commit (5741eb83b) replaced the approach: instead of reading the verdict prose, the review now reads a JSON block that reviewers and the judge are asked to append. That commit changes exactly the things the description rules out. The description also still documents the old approve-line rules and test names (`TestMaybePostReviewToTrailSkipsCleanVerdicts`).

Here's how the diff splits up.

**Required by the JSON-block approach** (in scope if you keep that approach, but the description has to say so):
- Reviewer and judge prompt changes (`prompt.go`, `synthesis_prompt.go`), plus the `TrailFindingsJSON` setting passed through `RunConfig`, `SynthesisSink` and `cmd.go`.
- `trail_report.go` and the `review_bridge.go` rewrite.
- Hiding the JSON block wherever output is shown (`dump.go`, `fix.go`, `synthesis_sink.go`). Otherwise every user would see the raw JSON.
- The Pi `Delta` flag. On `main` each streamed Pi fragment is joined with a newline, so a JSON line split mid-string would fail to parse. It's needed, but it changes how Pi text is joined in every mode, not just trail mode. That's why #1 belongs to this PR, and why I'd move the fix into the Pi parser (#7) rather than shared types.

**Beyond the stated goal ("don't post clean verdicts"):**
1. **Judge override (#4).** Reposting reviewer high-severity comments when the judge returns none is a new rule about how much to trust the judge, unrelated to clean verdicts. It's also the source of the duplicate-posting finding. I'd drop it, or make it its own PR.
2. **Structured findings without a judge.** Single-reviewer and no-judge runs now post native findings with severity and location from each reviewer's JSON, merged together. That's a feature upgrade: before, only the judge's last line was parsed as JSON. It's reasonable, but it's new behavior to describe or split out.
3. **`synthesisPromptOptions` refactor.** This one is fine. It's mechanical and needed for the new parameter.
4. **Branch name.** `fix-claude-review-stream-parser` comes from the parser bug that #2699 has since fixed. That's cosmetic, but reviewers may find it confusing.

**My recommendation:** keep the JSON-block approach. The five earlier commits were a series of special-case fixes to prose parsing, and the JSON block is the more robust fix. But:
- drop the judge override (#4);
- fix #1 inside the Pi parser instead of with the shared flag (#7);
- fix #2, #3 and #6;
- rewrite the title and description for what the PR actually does now, e.g. "fix(review): read trail findings from a JSON block instead of parsing verdict prose", including the prompt changes.

The alternative is to go back to f6d5376d2 or earlier for a smaller prose-only fix and open the JSON block as a follow-up PR. That's less to review, but it brings back the fragile prose parsing.

Which way do you want to go? If it's the first, I'll write the change plan and the new PR description for you to approve before I edit anything.

content.text:
Below is what I propose to change. I won't edit anything until you approve it.

**Fixes**

| # | Problem | Root cause (verified) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 + 7 | Pi messages run together in the joined text, so a verdict like `request changes` gets missed | The shared `Delta` flag joins every pair of adjacent deltas, even across message and retry boundaries | In `agent/pi/reviewer.go`, collect each message's deltas and emit one `AssistantText` at `message_end`. Also emit any leftover text if the stream ends early. Remove `Delta` from `types/reviewer.go` and go back to the plain newline join in `joinAssistantText`. |
| 2 | Labeled verdicts and feedback labels count as clean | 5741eb83b deleted `findings.go`, and `proseReportsFindings` only checks bare prefixes | Strip a leading `Verdict:` label before the verdict check. Bring back the feedback labels (`nits:`, `issues:`, `concerns:`, `suggestions:`) and the full set of severity markers (`[p0]`…`[p3]`, `[nit]`, `high:`, `P2 —`, …) from the deleted helpers, inside `trail_report.go`. |
| 3 | One blank comment throws away all the findings | `decodeTrailComments` returns ok=false when any entry has an empty body | Skip blank entries, as `main` did. If every entry is blank, treat it like `[]`, which still goes through the prose check. |
| 6 | Reviewer JSON reaches the judge twice | `composeSynthesisPrompt` embeds the raw narrative | Use `stripTrailJSON(joinAssistantText(...))` there. |
| 8 | Two copies of the severity rules have drifted | `isHighTrailSeverity` duplicates `normalizeReviewTrailSeverity` | Move the normalizer into the `review` package as `NormalizeTrailSeverity`. The bridge calls it, and `isHighTrailSeverity` is replaced by a check that it returns `"high"`. |
| 9 | Internal wording in user output | `why` is printed to the user | Drop the `why` return value. The user always sees the plain "Nothing to report" line, and the reason goes to `logging.Debug`. |

**Leaving #5 as is.** Removing malformed trailing JSON from posted prose is on purpose and documented, so I'd only add a test that locks it in.

**Order of work (tests first, per your rules)**
1. Add failing cases to `trail_report_test.go` and `pi/reviewer_test.go`, using the exact inputs I reproduced in the scratchpad: two messages separated by a tool call, a retry with partial output, `**Verdict:** request changes`, `Nits:`, `[p1]`, a blank body next to a real comment, and a judge prompt that must not contain reviewer JSON. Then run them and confirm they fail.
2. Make the production changes and update the docs section in `review-command.md`.
3. `mise run check`.

**Tradeoff to accept:** for Pi, the TUI preview and detail view would update once per message instead of per streamed token. That matches what the other reviewers emit, and the per-token preview only ever showed fragments anyway.

**One decision needed, #4 (judge override):**
- **(a) Drop the override (recommended).** If the judge returns `[]`, nothing is posted. This trusts the judge, matches its prompt ("drop unsupported claims"), and is the smallest, consistent fix. The risk is that a judge that wrongly returns `[]` hides a real high-severity finding.
- **(b) Keep the override, but dedup the highs** (by file, line and body) **and apply it whenever the judge didn't report them**, not only when it returned `[]`. This gives more safety, but it overrides the judge's filtering, adds more code, and takes the PR further from its stated goal.

Approve this plan, with (a) or (b) for #4?

cli.md
General.md
# General Review Lessons

- Make a guard's zero-match check count only the matches it is meant to protect. Matches that are always present, like the guard's own allowed cases, keep the check from ever firing.
- Test a guard by planting a violation and by breaking its detection, and see it fail both times. A guard that passes on clean code proves nothing.
- Before acting on a review finding, check whether existing tests or contracts explain the current shape. A structural test can be why the code looks the way it does.
- When code reads a user-owned config into a typed struct and writes it back, keep the fields it does not model. Any new reason to rewrite the file otherwise silently deletes user data.
- Make a new outer timeout longer than every internal budget on that path. Otherwise the kill fires before the code's own graceful fallback.
- Before setting an explicit timeout, look up the platform's current default for that exact event; an explicit value can shorten the budget rather than add one.
- When splitting known from unknown JSON keys to preserve them, decode only the exact known keys and keep every other key, case variants included, as unknown. `encoding/json` matches field names case-insensitively, so decoding the whole object lets a key like `"Command"` overwrite the real field.
- When a change makes a fix command riskier or changes which command to run, update every place that tells the user to run it (status, doctor, help text). Otherwise one screen sends people to the safe fix and the next to the destructive one.
# cli Review Lessons

- A capability guard must catch every way to reach a capability, including anonymous and local interfaces, not only the named interface. Go interfaces are structural, so a type assertion to any interface with the same method skips the `As*` gate.
- If `InstallHooks` can rewrite an agent's config without adding hooks, report it through `StaleHookReporter`. `count == 0` alone prints "already installed", which hides the rewrite.
- When a change alters what Entire writes into an agent's config, make it reach existing installs, not only new ones: users rarely re-run `entire enable`. Add an `entire doctor` repair for anything safe to fix silently, and check that doctor does not report the old config as OK.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

content.text:
The agreed fixes are in, and `mise run check` passes: format and lint are clean, unit and integration tests pass, and the Vogon (53/53) and roger-roger (4/4) canaries pass. Nothing is committed yet.

**What changed** (10 files, +203 / −116)
- **#1:** The Pi parser now sets `Delta` only on a fragment that continues the current message. It resets at `message_end` and `auto_retry_start`, so separate messages and retries start on a new line again. `joinAssistantText` adds a newline before every non-continuation event.
- **#2:** `proseReportsFindings` handles `Verdict:` labels again, plus `Nits:` / `Issues:` / `Concerns:` / `Suggestions:` and the full set of severity markers (`[p1]`, `P2:`, `high —`, …).
- **#3:** Comments with a blank body are skipped instead of invalidating the whole array.
- **#4:** The judge override is removed, along with `isHighTrailSeverity`. When a judge runs, its JSON alone decides what's posted.
- **#6:** The judge prompt now leaves out the reviewers' JSON lines.
- **#9:** The notice is always the plain "Nothing to report" line.
- The docs section in `review-command.md` is updated to match.

**Tests:** I wrote the new and changed tests first and confirmed they failed against the old code (8 label cases, blank body, judge override, notice wording, judge prompt, Pi boundaries). They all pass now.

**Differences from the plan:**
- For #9, I dropped the reason entirely instead of sending it to `logging.Debug`. Without the override, the only reason left for skipping is "no comments", so a log line wouldn't tell anyone anything.
- One case I noticed while writing it: a clean line that happens to start with a marker followed by a delimiter, like `Low - risk change.`, now posts. That fits the PR's rule of posting when unsure.

**Not verified:** a real `entire review` run in trail mode against a live trail. That needs paid agent calls, so I didn't run one.

**Commit message for your approval:**

```
fix(review): tighten the trail JSON contract checks

Keep streamed Pi text from different messages or retry attempts on
separate lines, so a verdict after a tool call still starts its own
line and the clean-review check sees it.

Treat labeled verdicts, feedback labels such as "Nits:", and priority
markers such as "[p1]" as findings when the comments array is empty.

Skip comments with a blank body instead of rejecting the whole array.

Let the judge's comments alone decide what is posted, drop reviewer
JSON lines from the judge prompt, and keep the "Nothing to report"
notice free of internal wording.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

**Rewritten PR description for your approval.** The current one describes the old prose-parsing approach.

> Trail: https://entire.io/gh/MuskanPaliwal/cli/trails/12
>
> When a review finds nothing, `entire review` in trail mode still posts the approval to the Trail as an "Unspecified finding".
>
> The poster had no structured way to tell a clean review from one with findings, so it fell back to posting the whole verdict as one whole-change comment. Earlier commits on this branch tried to recognize clean verdicts from prose, and each new phrasing needed another rule. This PR replaces that with an explicit output contract.
>
> ## What changed
>
> In trail mode only, reviewers and the judge end their output with one JSON line:
>
> ```json
> {"summary":"...","comments":[{"severity":"high","body":"...","location":{...}}]}
> ```
>
> The instruction comes last in the prompt, after profile and per-run text. It is not added for a verbatim `prompt` override. Posting reads this line:
>
> - `"comments":[]` posts nothing and prints "Nothing to report", unless the prose contradicts it with a list item, a severity marker (`[high]`, `[p1]`, `P2:`), a feedback label (`Nits:`, `Issues:`), or a `request changes` / `approve with nits` verdict (also when labeled `Verdict:`). In that case the prose is posted.
> - Comments post as native findings with their severity and location. Entries without a body are skipped.
> - When a judge runs, its line alone decides what is posted. Without a judge, each reviewer's line is read and the comments are merged.
> - A missing or malformed line posts the prose, with any trailing JSON removed, split into findings by top-level bullet. When unsure, it posts.
>
> The JSON line is hidden wherever results are shown (live output, `entire review` detail, the judge's input) and kept in the saved manifest.
>
> Pi streams text as fragments. On `main` every fragment became its own line, which would split the JSON line. Fragments of one message now join without a separator, and each new message or retry attempt starts a new line.
>
> ## Scope
>
> This changes the reviewer and judge prompts in trail mode only. Local output, reviewer failure policy, Trail API types, and server rendering are unchanged.
>
> ## Tests
>
> - `review/trail_report_test.go`: clean and non-clean judge and reviewer outputs, fenced and pretty-printed JSON, malformed contracts, labeled verdicts and feedback labels, blank-body comments, a judge `[]` alongside a reviewer finding, and streamed fragments across messages.
> - `agent/pi/reviewer_test.go`: fragment continuation resets at each message and retry.
> - `review/synthesis_prompt_test.go`: the trail-mode judge prompt ends with the contract, and reviewer JSON is not repeated in the judge's input.
>
> 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

Once you approve, I'll commit, run `mise run lint` again, push, update the PR description, and check the trail findings. Both texts avoid em dashes; the `—` in the commit message's quoted test strings isn't there.

**Proposed review lesson** for `Review Lessons/cli.md`, still waiting on your approval:
- "When rewriting a parser or classifier, keep the earlier fixes' regression cases (for example, feedback labels like `Nits:`) as tests for the new implementation; a rewrite can silently drop handling that only those cases cover."

Do you approve the commit message, the PR description and the lesson?

`joinAssistantText` only looks at the previous *AssistantText* event's `Delta` flag, not whether anything occurred in between. A `ToolCall` (or any other non-`AssistantText` event) between two delta-streamed messages doesn't reset `prevDelta`, so the last fragment of one assistant message and the first fragment of the next get concatenated with no separator. For Pi, which is the only adapter setting `Delta: true`, a tool call commonly separates two distinct assistant messages (e.g. reasoning text, then a tool call, then the verdict/JSON message) — these would be glued together, corrupting the narrative shown in `dump.go`/`SynthesisSink` output and potentially breaking `splitTrailJSON`'s line-based scan if the trailing JSON line gets fused onto unrelated prose.
